name: Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds
description: Werner’s theory, ligands and terms, IUPAC names, isomerism, VBT, crystal field splitting, colour, metal carbonyls and applications

cards.term: Chlorophyll, haemoglobin, vitamin B₁₂: central metals?
cards.definition: Mg, Fe, Co
Metallurgy, industrial catalysts, analytical reagents, electroplating, textile dyeing, medicine

cards.term: What did Werner observe with CoCl₃·xNH₃ and AgNO₃?
cards.definition: Different numbers of Cl⁻ precipitated as AgCl in the cold: only ionisable Cl⁻ reacts

cards.text: Moles of AgCl per mole: CoCl₃·6NH₃ (yellow) = {{c1::3}}; CoCl₃·5NH₃ (purple) = {{c2::2}}; CoCl₃·4NH₃ (green and violet) = {{c3::1}}.

cards.term: Werner formulas and electrolyte types for the cobalt ammines?
cards.definition: [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ 1:3; [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ 1:2; [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]Cl 1:1 (green and violet are isomers)

cards.term: Intuition: how does AgNO₃ "count" bracket vs outside Cl⁻?
cards.definition: Cl⁻ outside the bracket is free in solution and grabs Ag⁺; Cl⁻ inside is held by the metal and can’t
Ionisable; satisfied by negative ions (= oxidation state in modern terms)
Non-ionisable; satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions; = coordination number, fixed for a metal

cards.term: What did Werner say about the secondary linkages’ arrangement?
cards.definition: Characteristic spatial arrangements (coordination polyhedra): octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar most common
Octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar

cards.term: Secondary valences: PdCl₂·4NH₃ (2 AgCl), NiCl₂·6H₂O (2), PtCl₄·2HCl (0), CoCl₃·4NH₃ (1), PtCl₂·2NH₃ (0)? (Example 5.1)
cards.definition: 4, 6, 6, 6, 4
Double salts (carnallite, Mohr’s salt, potash alum) dissociate completely in water; complex ions like [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ do not
Swiss chemist (1866–1919), first to find optical activity in coordination compounds; first Swiss chemist to win the Nobel Prize (1913)
Central metal atom/ion bonded to a fixed number of ions/molecules, e.g. [CoCl₃(NH₃)₃], [Ni(CO)₄], [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻
Ni²⁺, Co³⁺, Fe³⁺; they act as Lewis acids
Ions/molecules bound to the central atom: Cl⁻, H₂O, NH₃, en, N(CH₂CH₂NH₂)₃, even proteins; they are Lewis bases (electron-pair donors)

cards.text: Denticity: Cl⁻, H₂O, NH₃ are {{c1::unidentate}}; en and C₂O₄²⁻ are {{c2::didentate}}; N(CH₂CH₂NH₂)₃ is {{c3::polydentate}}; EDTA⁴⁻ is {{c4::hexadentate}}.

cards.definition: 2 N + 4 O (hexadentate)

cards.term: What is a chelate ligand? Why are chelates more stable?
cards.definition: A di/polydentate ligand binding one metal through ≥ 2 donors; ring formation makes chelate complexes more stable

cards.term: Intuition: why are chelates extra stable?
cards.definition: Like a crab’s claw (Greek chele): if one "finger" lets go, the other still holds the metal, so it clicks back instead of floating away

cards.term: What is an ambidentate ligand? Examples?
cards.definition: Two different donor atoms, either can bind: NO₂⁻ (N or O), SCN⁻ (S or N)
Number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal (count σ bonds only, not π)
6, 4, 6, 6 (oxalate and en are didentate)
No: 3 en × 2 donor atoms = 6

cards.term: Coordination sphere and counter ions in K₄[Fe(CN)₆]?
cards.definition: Sphere: [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻; counter ion: K⁺
Spatial arrangement of donor atoms around the central atom

cards.term: Oxidation number of the central atom: definition?
cards.definition: Charge left on the metal if all ligands are removed with their shared electron pairs; e.g. Cu in [Cu(CN)₄]³⁻ = +1, written Cu(I)
Charge of complex − sum of ligand charges. [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺: x − 1 = +2 → Co(+3)
Homoleptic: one kind of donor group, [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺. Heteroleptic: more than one kind, [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺.

cards.text: Formula rules: {{c1::central atom}} first; then ligands in {{c2::alphabetical}} order (charge ignored); whole entity in {{c3::square brackets}}; polyatomic ligands in {{c4::parentheses}}.

cards.term: How is charge written on a complex ion formula?
cards.definition: Right superscript outside the bracket, number before sign: [Co(CN)₆]³⁻, [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺

cards.term: Order when naming a complex compound?
cards.definition: Cation first, then anion; inside the entity, ligands alphabetically before the metal (reverse of formula writing)

cards.text: Ligand names: anionic end in {{c1::-o / -ido}} (chlorido, cyanido); H₂O = {{c2::aqua}}; NH₃ = {{c3::ammine}}; CO = {{c4::carbonyl}}; NO = {{c5::nitrosyl}}.

cards.term: When are bis, tris, tetrakis used?
cards.definition: When the ligand name already has a numerical prefix: dichloridobis(triphenylphosphine)nickel(II) for [NiCl₂(PPh₃)₂]

cards.term: Metal name in a complex anion?
cards.definition: Ends in -ate (cobaltate); Latin names for some: ferrate (Fe), cuprate, argentate, aurate, plumbate

tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate

cards.term: Two main types of isomerism in coordination compounds?
cards.definition: Stereoisomerism (geometrical, optical) and structural (linkage, coordination, ionisation, solvate)
Stereo: same bonds, different spatial arrangement. Structural: different bonds.
cis (X adjacent) and trans (X opposite)

cards.term: How many isomers for square planar [MABXL]?
cards.definition: 3: two cis, one trans

cards.term: Why no geometrical isomers for tetrahedral complexes? (Example 5.4)
cards.definition: All four positions are adjacent to each other, so relative positions are identical
cis (Cl at 90°) and trans (Cl at 180°)
cis and trans
fac: three same ligands on one face. mer: around the meridian.
fac: the three identical ligands form a triangle (all mutually 90°). mer: they lie in a line/arc (one pair at 180°).
cis and trans (the two NH₃ adjacent or opposite)
Non-superimposable mirror images (chiral); d rotates plane-polarised light right, l left
Octahedral complexes with didentate ligands, e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺

cards.term: Which isomer of [PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ is optically active?
cards.definition: Only cis (trans has a mirror plane)

cards.term: Which is chiral: cis- or trans-[CrCl₂(ox)₂]³⁻? (Example 5.6)
cards.definition: cis; trans has a plane of symmetry

cards.term: Intuition: quick chirality test for M(AA)₂X₂?
cards.definition: Trans: the plane through the two chelates is a mirror → achiral. Cis: chelates twist like a propeller → chiral
Ambidentate ligand: [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ is red when bound via O (–ONO), yellow via N (–NO₂) (Jørgensen)
Ligands swap between cationic and anionic metals: [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆]
Counter ion and a ligand swap: [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄
BaCl₂ gives white BaSO₄ only with the first; AgNO₃ gives AgCl only with the second
[Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) and [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (grey-green): water inside vs outside the sphere

[Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]²⁺ vs [Co(NH₃)₅(ONO)]²⁺: Linkage; [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] vs [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆]: Coordination; [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br vs [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄: Ionisation; [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ vs [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O: Solvate (hydrate); cis vs trans-[Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺: Geometrical; d vs l-[Co(en)₃]³⁺: Optical

sp³d², outer orbital, high spin, paramagnetic

cards.term: Inner orbital vs outer orbital complex?
cards.definition: Inner (low spin, spin paired): uses (n−1)d, d²sp³. Outer (high spin, spin free): uses nd, sp³d².
sp³, tetrahedral, paramagnetic (2 unpaired; Ni²⁺ 3d⁸)
Ni is in the 0 state (3d¹⁰ after CO forces 4s electrons into 3d): no unpaired electrons, sp³
dsp², square planar, diamagnetic (CN⁻ pairs the 3d⁸ electrons)
0 (Pt²⁺ d⁸, dsp²)
No: hybridisation is a mathematical manipulation of wave equations

cards.term: Why d¹–d³ ions behave the same free and complexed (octahedral)?
cards.definition: Two 3d orbitals are already vacant for d²sp³, so no pairing is needed
A vacant pair of 3d orbitals needs pairing, leaving 2, 1 or 0 unpaired electrons (d⁴, d⁵, d⁶)

cards.term: Which of those are inner orbital (d²sp³) complexes?
cards.definition: [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻, [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, [Co(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻

cards.term: Why is [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ strongly but [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ weakly paramagnetic? (Intext 5.7)
cards.definition: H₂O weak: 5 unpaired (sp³d²). CN⁻ strong: pairs electrons, 1 unpaired (d²sp³).

cards.term: Why is [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ inner orbital but [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ outer? (Intext 5.8)
cards.definition: Co³⁺ (d⁶) can pair to free two 3d orbitals; Ni²⁺ (d⁸) cannot free two 3d, so it must use 4d (sp³d²)
Tetrahedral (sp³): 5 unpaired electrons, so no dsp² pairing
Measure μ → \( n \) from \( \mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} \) → which orbitals are free → hybridisation and shape

cards.text: Limitations of VBT: many {{c1::assumptions}}; no quantitative {{c2::magnetic}} data; cannot explain {{c3::colour}}; no quantitative stability; can’t predict {{c4::tetrahedral vs square planar}}; doesn’t distinguish {{c5::weak and strong ligands}}.

cards.term: Basic assumption of crystal field theory?
cards.definition: Metal–ligand bond is purely ionic/electrostatic; ligands are point charges (anions) or point dipoles (neutral)

cards.term: When do d orbitals stay degenerate?
cards.definition: In a free ion or a spherically symmetric field; a ligand field is asymmetric and splits them

cards.term: Which d orbitals point at the ligands?
cards.definition: dx²−y² and dz² point along the axes at the ligands (e_g, raised); dxy, dyz, dxz point between them (t2g, lowered)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
What the d-orbital labels mean

Ligands sit on the x and y axes. Which orbital is repelled more, A or B? Name both.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
What the d-orbital labels mean

Ligands sit on the x and y axes. Which orbital is repelled more, A or B? Name both.

A = dx²−y²: eg, upB = dxy: t2g, down
Read the subscript. x²−y²: lobes lie along the x and y axes, head-on into the ligands. xy: lobes lie between x and y, dodging them. dz² points along z (also eg); dyz and dxz lie between axes (t2g).

cards.term: What do the orbital labels xy, yz, xz, x²−y², z² tell you?
cards.definition: Where the lobes point: xy, yz, xz → between two axes; x²−y² → along x and y; z² → along z (plus a ring)

cards.term: What do t₂g and e_g mean?
cards.definition: t = triply degenerate (3 orbitals), e = doubly degenerate (2); g (gerade) = symmetric through the centre
d orbitals split into e_g (dx²−y², dz²; up by 3/5 Δo) and t2g (dxy, dyz, dxz; down by 2/5 Δo)

eg: 2 go upt2g: 3 go downgap = Δ₀
Lobes pointing at ligands (eg) are repelled most and rise by 3/5 Δ₀; lobes between ligands (t2g) drop by 2/5 Δ₀. The average stays put: 2 × 3/5 = 3 × 2/5.

cards.definition: e_g up by 3/5 Δ₀, t₂g down by 2/5 Δ₀

I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO

No: it is found experimentally from light absorption

cards.term: Weak vs strong field ligands: the rule of thumb?
cards.definition: Halides at the weak end; C-donors (CN⁻, CO) at the strong end; O-donors weak-ish, N-donors stronger
Energy needed to put two electrons in the same orbital
t₂g³e_g¹: weak field, high spin
t₂g⁴e_g⁰: strong field, low spin
Weak field, Δo < P: t2g³eg¹, high spin (4 unpaired). Strong field, Δo > P: t2g⁴, low spin (2 unpaired).

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
High spin vs low spin

A d⁴ ion has 3 electrons in t₂g. Where does the 4th go: weak vs strong field ligand?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
High spin vs low spin

A d⁴ ion has 3 electrons in t₂g. Where does the 4th go: weak vs strong field ligand?

Δ₀ < P: climbing up is cheaper than pairing, so the electron goes up: high spin. Δ₀ > P: pairing is cheaper: low spin.
Like a bus: sit alone upstairs if the stairs (Δ₀) cost less than squeezing into a shared seat (P).

cards.term: Which dⁿ configurations are more stable in strong fields (NCERT)?
cards.definition: d⁴ to d⁷

cards.term: Why can only d⁴–d⁷ be high or low spin (octahedral)?
cards.definition: d¹–d³ fill t₂g singly either way; d⁸–d¹⁰ have t₂g full, so the arrangement is forced; only d⁴–d⁷ face the "climb or pair" choice

cards.term: Mn²⁺: 5 unpaired with H₂O but 1 with CN⁻. Why? (Intext 5.10)
cards.definition: H₂O weak (Δ₀ < P): t₂g³e_g² (5 unpaired). CN⁻ strong (Δ₀ > P): t₂g⁵ (1 unpaired).
Tetrahedral splitting is inverted (e lower, t2 higher) and smaller: Δt = 4/9 Δo, so low spin is rare

invertedΔₜ = 4/9 Δ₀high spin
Only 4 ligands, and none point straight at a d lobe, so the pattern is upside down and small: never big enough to force pairing. No "g": a tetrahedron has no centre of symmetry.

cards.definition: Inverted; Δt = 4/9 Δ₀

cards.term: Why are low-spin tetrahedral complexes rare?
cards.definition: Δt = 4/9 Δ₀ is too small to force pairing

cards.term: Why no "g" in tetrahedral labels (e, t₂)?
cards.definition: Tetrahedral complexes lack a centre of symmetry
It absorbs part of visible light; we see the complementary colour (absorbs green → looks red)
Its one d electron jumps t₂g → e_g (d–d transition) by absorbing blue-green light (498 nm)

cards.definition: Table 5.3

cards.term: Intuition: why does a stronger ligand shift colour toward yellow?
cards.definition: Bigger Δ₀ needs higher-energy (shorter λ, bluer) light; removing blue/violet leaves a yellow-orange look

cards.term: Why is anhydrous CuSO₄ white but CuSO₄·5H₂O blue?
cards.definition: No ligand (water) → no splitting → no d–d transition. Same for [Ti(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ heated.

cards.text: Adding en to [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ ({{c1::green}}): 1 en → {{c2::pale blue}}; 2 en → {{c3::blue/purple}}; 3 en ([Ni(en)₃]²⁺) → {{c4::violet}}.

cards.term: Identify the trend in these tubes.
cards.definition: More en replacing H₂O raises Δ₀: [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ green → [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ violet
Al₂O₃ with 0.5–1% Cr³⁺ (d³) in octahedral sites: d–d transitions
Cr³⁺ in octahedral sites of beryl Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈: bands shift to longer λ (yellow-red, blue), so green is transmitted
Treating ligands as point charges predicts anions should split most, but anions are at the weak end; ignores covalent character
Ligand field theory and molecular orbital theory

cards.term: Insight: why is CO the strongest-field ligand though it is neutral?
cards.definition: π back-bonding: metal d electrons flow into CO’s π*, strengthening M–C and widening Δ₀; a covalent effect CFT ignores
Compounds with only CO ligands, formed by most transition metals
Two square pyramidal Mn(CO)₅ units joined by an Mn–Mn bond
Co–Co bond bridged by two CO groups

cards.term: σ part of the M–CO bond?
cards.definition: Lone pair on carbon donated into a vacant metal orbital

cards.term: π part of the M–CO bond?
cards.definition: Filled metal d orbital donates into the vacant antibonding π* of CO
σ donation and π back-donation reinforce each other, strengthening the M–CO bond
Like two friends lending money back and forth: CO gives the metal electron density (σ), the metal gives it back (π); each gift makes the next easier

cards.term: Consequence of back-bonding for the C≡O bond?
cards.definition: Electrons in CO’s π* weaken the C–O bond (lower C–O stretching frequency) while M–C strengthens

cards.term: Analytical reagents that form coloured complexes?
cards.definition: EDTA, DMG (dimethylglyoxime), α-nitroso-β-naphthol, cupron
Titration with Na₂EDTA (Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ complexes; selectivity from different stability constants)

cards.term: Complex in gold extraction, and recovery?
cards.definition: [Au(CN)₂]⁻ (Au + CN⁻ + O₂ + H₂O); gold recovered by adding zinc
Impure Ni → [Ni(CO)₄] → decomposed to pure Ni
Cyanocobalamine, Co; the anti-pernicious anaemia factor
Carboxypeptidase A, carbonic anhydrase
[(Ph₃P)₃RhCl]: hydrogenation of alkenes

cards.term: Why electroplate Ag and Au from [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ and [Au(CN)₂]⁻?
cards.definition: Gives a smoother, more even coating than simple metal ions

cards.term: Role of hypo in black-and-white photography?

cards.text: Chelate therapy: excess Cu and Fe removed by {{c1::D-penicillamine}} and {{c2::desferrioxime B}}; lead poisoning treated with {{c3::EDTA}}; tumours inhibited by {{c4::cis-platin}}.
